result: A two-step CRISPR/Cas9 genome editing strategy was developed to introduce cancer-associated TERT promoter mutations at the endogenous locus in human embryonic stem cells. The first step deleted a 1.5 kb region creating telomerase-negative cells (TERT∆/∆) that died after ~140 days, and the second step reintroduced the region with or without promoter mutations, generating isogenic cell lines differing only at the TERT promoter.
evaluation: Claims C25-C31 and C87-C92 describe a well-validated methodological approach with appropriate controls (Southern blot, PCR sequencing, telomere length assays, TRAP assays). The two-step strategy overcame technical challenges and successfully generated isogenic cell lines, as evidenced by Figures 1A-D and supplementary data. The approach is internally consistent and properly controlled.

result: In hESCs, the -124C/T TERT promoter mutation resulted in a 2-3 fold increase in TERT mRNA expression compared to wild-type controls, while the -57A/C and -146C/T mutations showed no significant increase. Despite elevated TERT mRNA in -124C/T cells, telomerase activity was not significantly increased.
evaluation: Claims C2, C20-C21, C32-C34, C65-C66, and C93 are supported by qRT-PCR data (Figure 1E) and TRAP assays (Figure 1F) showing differential effects of the three mutations on TERT expression in hESCs. The data are consistent across independent experiments and cell lines (Figure 1—figure supplements 2-3). The lack of increased telomerase activity despite increased TERT mRNA is a key observation.

result: In hESCs, TR (telomerase RNA) rather than TERT is the limiting component for telomerase activity. Overexpression of TR strongly increased telomerase activity and telomere elongation in hESCs, while TERT overexpression did not. Upon differentiation to fibroblasts or NPCs, TERT became limiting instead of TR.
evaluation: Claims C22, C35-C40, and C70 are well-supported by overexpression experiments shown in Figure 2. Northern blot (Figure 2B), Western blot (Figure 2C), TRAP assays (Figure 2D), and telomere length measurements (Figure 2E) provide converging evidence. The cell-type-specific switching of the limiting component is demonstrated by comparing hESCs to differentiated cells. This is a critical mechanistic finding explaining why TERT promoter mutations have minimal effect in hESCs.

result: Upon differentiation to fibroblasts, wild-type cells efficiently silenced TERT expression, but all three TERT promoter mutations prevented this silencing. Cells with -57A/C or -146C/T mutations showed 4-fold increased TERT expression, while -124C/T cells showed 8-12-fold increases. This aberrant TERT expression resulted in robust telomerase activity in differentiated fibroblasts carrying promoter mutations, while wild-type fibroblasts had undetectable telomerase activity.
evaluation: Claims C3, C23, C41-C51, C72, and C94 are strongly supported by qRT-PCR data (Figures 3A-D), TRAP assays (Figure 3E), and supplementary data (Figure 3—figure supplements 1-2). The data show consistent failure to silence TERT across multiple time points (up to 45 days), independent cell lines, and clonal populations. Differentiation markers (OCT4, COL1A1) confirm proper differentiation, ruling out impaired differentiation as an explanation.

result: TERT promoter mutations prevented TERT silencing in neural precursor cells (NPCs) and terminally differentiated neurons, resulting in robust telomerase activity. This effect persisted even in post-mitotic neurons treated with mitotic inhibitors for up to 1 month after terminal differentiation.
evaluation: Claims C52-C55 and C95 are supported by qRT-PCR data (Figures 4A, 4C), TRAP assays (Figure 4D), and immunofluorescence (Figure 4B) showing proper neuronal differentiation. The persistence of telomerase activity in non-dividing neurons is particularly striking and well-documented. Supplementary data (Figure 4—figure supplement 1) confirm findings in independent clones.

result: Differentiated cells with TERT promoter mutations exhibited telomerase activity levels comparable to immortal cancer cell lines. The -124C/T NPCs had telomerase activity equivalent to HeLa S3 cells and ~50% of hESCs, while -124C/T fibroblasts had 25-50% of the activity found in various cancer cell lines. All differentiated cell lines with promoter mutations showed increased telomere length compared to wild-type controls.
evaluation: Claims C24, C56-C59 are supported by comparative TRAP assays (Figures 5A-B) and telomere restriction fragment assays (Figures 5C-D and Figure 5—figure supplement 1A). The direct comparison to established cancer cell lines provides important context for the functional significance of the observed telomerase activity levels. The telomere length data demonstrate functional consequences of sustained telomerase activity.

result: In teratoma formation assays, cells with TERT promoter mutations maintained aberrantly long telomeres compared to wild-type controls. The -124C/T mutation showed the strongest effect, retaining telomere lengths nearly identical to undifferentiated hESCs. This demonstrates that TERT promoter mutations alone are sufficient to suppress telomere erosion without additional tumor-selected changes.
evaluation: Claims C60-C64 are supported by teratoma formation assays and telomere restriction fragment analysis (Figure 5E and Figure 5—figure supplement 1B). The in vivo teratoma model provides an unbiased assessment of long-term differentiation and telomere maintenance. All cell lines formed teratomas of similar size, controlling for proliferation differences. The data demonstrate causality between TERT promoter mutations and telomere maintenance in a complex in vivo differentiation context.

result: TERT promoter mutations are sufficient to overcome the proliferative barrier imposed by telomere shortening without additional tumor-selected mutations, and can promote immortalization and tumorigenesis of incipient cancer cells. The underlying mechanism is failure to repress telomerase upon differentiation into somatic cells.
evaluation: Claims C4-C5, C73-C75 represent the main conclusions of the study and are well-supported by the collective experimental evidence from differentiation experiments (Figures 3-5), telomerase activity assays, and telomere length measurements. The use of isogenic cell lines differing only at the TERT promoter is critical for establishing sufficiency. The mechanistic insight about failure of silencing rather than activation is novel and well-supported.

result: There is a strong positional effect between the location of TERT promoter mutations and the core transcription initiation machinery. Despite creating the same ETS-binding motif (TTCCGG), mutations at different positions have different effects on TERT transcription. All cancer-associated promoter mutations are located in close proximity to the transcriptional start site.
evaluation: Claims C67 and C69 are supported by the differential effects of the three mutations observed in Figure 1E, despite all creating the same binding motif. However, C68 is speculative about why a mutation at position -89 is not observed in cancer. The positional effect observation is valid and important, but the mechanistic explanation remains incomplete. The speculation about the -89 position lacks experimental support.

result: Immortal hESCs are as uninformative with regard to cancer-associated TERT mutations as immortal tumor tissue or cell lines.
evaluation: Claim C71 is supported by the observation that TERT is not limiting in hESCs (Figure 2), making them unsuitable for studying the functional impact of TERT promoter mutations. This is an important methodological insight that explains why previous studies using tumor cell lines may have been limited. The claim is well-justified by the experimental data.

result: The authors propose a model to explain the tumor spectrum of TERT promoter mutations. In tissues with telomerase-positive stem cells and long telomeres (e.g., bone marrow, intestine), TERT promoter mutations may be neutral. In contrast, in telomerase-negative cells with short telomeres (e.g., melanocytes, hepatocytes), TERT promoter mutations provide an immediate proliferative advantage by bypassing the Hayflick limit.
evaluation: Claims C76-C82 present a speculative model illustrated in Figure 6. While C76-C77 are supported by citations to prior literature, C78-C82 are largely inferential and speculative. The model is plausible and consistent with the experimental findings, but lacks direct experimental validation in the relevant tissue types. The model makes testable predictions but requires additional work to confirm. The speculation is reasonable but not experimentally demonstrated in this study.

result: The isogenic cell line model system provides a platform for identifying therapeutic approaches specific to TERT promoter mutations. Targeting TERT promoter mutations is attractive because they are exclusive to tumor cells and not present in surrounding normal tissue, potentially allowing selective targeting of tumor cells without affecting telomerase-positive adult stem cells.
evaluation: Claims C83-C86 discuss therapeutic implications but are largely speculative. C83 is partially supported by the experimental demonstration that mutations are sufficient to de-repress TERT. C84 correctly describes the utility of the model system. However, C85-C86 are speculative about therapeutic selectivity without experimental validation. No therapeutic interventions were tested in this study. These claims represent reasonable future directions but lack experimental support.

result: Background claims about TERT promoter mutations in cancer, telomerase biology, and prior characterization of these mutations from the literature.
evaluation: Claims C1, C6-C19, and C36 are background information supported by appropriate citations to prior literature. These claims establish the context and rationale for the study. The citations appear appropriate and the claims are consistent with established knowledge in the field.
